The excerpt provides a comparison between an on-line wall friction tester and a Jenike-type wall friction tester, but it does not discuss inclined-plane or tilting-plate measurements, Schulze ring shear testing, or wall adhesion explicitly. For crushed glass and coal, the on-line tester produced significantly higher wall-friction angles than the Jenike tester, for both initially clean and subsequently unclean wall conditions. Wall condition strongly affected the results: an unclean stainless-steel plate gave higher wall-friction values, attributed to bulk solid embedding into the wall surface. Cleaning the plate reduced friction to the initial shear-stress value, while repeated testing showed that plate wear was not the main cause. The measurements also show a displacement-dependent evolution: an initial approximately constant region, a transient increase, and a final steady-state value after roughly 150 m of shear displacement. During the transient stage, friction increased at a rate dependent on speed, while load had less influence; the excerpt does not establish a quantitative stress dependence of wall-friction angle over 50–500 Pa. The authors emphasize that Jenike testing has limited displacement (about 10 mm) and therefore may not reproduce a naturally embedded, unclean wall condition without manually rubbing material into the wall.

The excerpt compares Jenike and Schulze ring shear wall-friction measurements, but it does not discuss inclined-plane or tilting-plate methods, nor does it define wall adhesion. For the tested soft PE pellets and wall plates, the two shear testers generally produced similar wall-friction angles when wall roughness and other testing conditions were comparable. The reported exception occurred at low pressure, specifically 500 Pa, indicating that agreement between methods may deteriorate in the low-normal-stress range relevant to the question. The article represents wall behavior using a wall yield locus, generally described as a curved line; consequently, wall friction angle is not necessarily constant and varies as a function of pressure at the wall. The excerpt identifies wall roughness as the most important parameter in the study: decreasing roughness decreased wall-friction angles for both testers. Jenike testing is described as translational and operator-dependent, whereas the Schulze ring shear tester provides automated measurement. The supplied pages do not provide results at 50 Pa, do not compare either tester with a tilting-plate test, and do not provide enough information to quantify stress dependence or establish an adhesion value.

Powder Technology, 174:64-70, May 2007. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2006.10.024, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2006.10.024. This article has 23 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes a comparison between an on-line wall-friction tester and a Jenike wall-friction tester, using crushed glass and coal against stainless-steel wall material. It does not discuss inclined-plane or tilting-plate measurements specifically, nor does it provide a comparison with Schulze ring-shear wall-friction tests. The on-line device uses a skid plate resting on, or shearing against, a controlled bed of bulk solid transported by a conveyor; a load cell measures the shear force. The conveyor controls shear velocity over 0.01–1.23 m/s, and the study examines how velocity or shear displacement affects the measured wall-friction angle. The stated objectives include evaluating correlation between on-line and off-line wall-friction measurements. The excerpt also explains that conventional Jenike and annular shear-cell methods are time-consuming, require sample preparation, and provide neither immediate nor continuous indication of flowability; small off-line samples may not represent an entire batch. No numerical data are given here for low normal stresses of 50–500 Pa, no stress-dependence relationship for wall-friction angle is reported in these pages, and wall adhesion is not defined or quantified. Therefore, the excerpt supports only a general methodological comparison with Jenike testing, not conclusions about inclined-plane versus Jenike/Schulze results or adhesion.

Abstract:
This study examined the feasibility of combining data from different powder flow testers to determine the flow function characteristics of pharmaceutical powders. The Brookfield PFT and Freeman FT4 can measure flow function over different scales of consolidation load but were found to be most complementary with CRM limestone powder and lactose. The brittle behaviour of Easytab particles at higher loads made obtaining repeatable results with the FT4 challenging. By using the method of Wang et al., where the flow function coefficient ffc is plotted against the dimensionless cohesion C* (measured cohesion Ta divided by the initial compaction I), a plot was formed which could be used to predict the behaviour of other systems, which compared well with previous studies.

The excerpt provides partial information relevant to uniaxial compression testing and comparison with shear-cell methods. It identifies uniaxial compression in a consolidometer or oedometer as a basic way to measure powder compressibility, using the relationship between powder volume, void ratio, or displacement and logarithmic applied stress. For the Johanson Indicizer, a cylindrical test cell and two-part piston consolidate the sample; after the lower support is removed, the inner piston drives failure and measures empirical strength. A correction factor of approximately 2.2 is applied to estimate unconﬁned yield strength. Johanson reported that the method generates a powder flow function in roughly one-tenth the time of the Jenike test, but multiple researchers questioned whether its failure stress truly represents unconﬁned yield strength, and comparisons found often smaller yield-strength, arching, and rathole values than Jenike and Peschl shear cells. The excerpt also notes that wall friction affects testing: the POSTEC tester uses a flexible membrane to compact samples homogeneously and reduce specimen–die friction, producing slightly lower fc values than Jenike-type shear cells and a biaxial tester. The excerpt describes the uniaxial compression method for measuring powder unconfined yield strength (σc). Powder is placed in a hollow cylinder, consolidated vertically by a piston, unloaded, and dismantled to produce a self-supporting powder column. The column is then loaded until failure, with the failure stress taken as the unconfined yield strength. Increasing consolidation stress generally increases powder strength and σc. The test provides good control of consolidation stress and strain rate and is useful for quality control and flowability ranking. However, it requires sufficient cohesion and consolidation to form a stable, free-standing column, so it is unsuitable for very low-stress measurements. It cannot directly determine wall friction or internal friction, and wall friction in the mould reduces the measured strength; consequently, the result is often termed the uniaxial unconfined yield strength. Compared with uniaxial compression, shear-cell testing establishes a reproducible steady-state or critically consolidated condition and can generate yield loci, Mohr circles, unconfined yield strength, flowability index, and internal friction angle. The excerpt states that uniaxial testing may underestimate strength and bulk density relative to shear testing at comparable stresses. Shear cells are themselves mainly suited to moderate-to-high stresses because pre-shear must exceed the lowest applied stress. The excerpt does not discuss height-to-diameter ratio, specific mould geometry, or the Williams and Birks, Parrella, Freeman, Brookfield PFT, Ezi-Tester, or Johanson Indicizer apparatuses.

The excerpt describes cylindrical mould and uniaxial compression methods for determining powder unconﬁned yield strength and constructing a failure function. A key consideration is the specimen length-to-diameter ratio (L/D). Wall friction produces nonuniform vertical pressure and bulk density, potentially causing failure at the weakest region; therefore, L/D should be minimized to reduce stress variation. However, L/D must exceed a critical value so the failure plane does not intersect an end plate. Although a value near unity was proposed under a 45° failure-plane assumption, actual slip planes may require a larger ratio. Experimental findings cited in the excerpt indicate that end-plate slippage becomes negligible when L/D exceeds 2. Direct mould testers use uniaxial compaction, but nonuniform voidage can limit steady-state deformation and introduce inaccuracies. The Williams unconﬁned compression test addresses wall-friction effects by forming a freestanding powder column in a segmented, split mould. Powder is compacted incrementally, generally under consolidation stresses above 100 kPa, and the mould is removed before applying timed increasing weights until breakage. The measured breakage stress is the unconﬁned yield stress for that consolidation stress; repeating the test at different stresses provides the failure function. The excerpt does not discuss shear-cell flow-function comparisons or the Parrella, Freeman, Brookfield PFT, Ezi-Tester, or Johanson Indicizer instruments.

The excerpt describes the uniaxial compression test for determining powder unconfined yield strength. A powder column is consolidated vertically under stress σ1, the consolidating load is removed, and the unsupported column is compressed until failure. Because the lateral surface is unconfined, the minor principal stress is effectively zero; the failure stress is the unconfined yield strength, σc. The flow function coefficient is ffc = σ1/σc, with larger values indicating better flowability. Jenike’s classifications are: ffc < 1, not flowing; 1–2, very cohesive; 2–4, cohesive; 4–10, easy flowing; and >10, free flowing. Bulk density and unconfined yield strength generally increase with consolidation stress. The method is simple, rapid, inexpensive, and useful for quality control, but free-flowing powders may not form stable columns and high consolidation stresses may not represent low-stress industrial conditions. Wall friction may produce nonuniform density and underestimate strength. The excerpt also contrasts shear-cell testing: Jenike cells quantify shear resistance and flow properties but have limited displacement, while ring shear testers provide unlimited strain and require pre-consolidation and pre-shearing. Abstract:
While targeted alignment in certain additive manufacturing (AM) methods such as material extrusion (MEX) and stereolithography (SLA) has been well documented in the research community, a method for targeted alignment of added fillers or fibrous materials in powder bed fusion (PBF) AM devices has yet to be successfully achieved. Similarly, incorporation of multimaterials does not work easily with any of the AM technologies. This study creates a prototype design that could be integrated into a PBF system to allow for multimaterial layer deposition and alignment of powders and powder blends. Different concept designs, multichambered and multi-hopper with hopper angles calculated specifically for the composite blend powders selected, were proposed. Initial deposition trials outside a PBF process were tested, and the deposited layers were measured.

Abstract:
Dry powder coating is used in many industries to tailor the bulk solid characteristics of cohesive powders. Within this paper, the state of the art of dry coating of feedstock materials for powder based additive manufacturing (AM) processes will be reviewed. The focus is on feedstock materials for powder bed fusion AM processes, such as powder bed fusion of polymers with a laser beam and powder bed fusion of metals with lasers or an electron beam. Powders of several microns to several ten microns in size are used and the feedstock’s bulk solid properties, especially the flowability and packing density are of immanent importance in different process steps in particular for powder dosing and spreading of powder layers onto the building area. All these properties can be tuned by dry particle coating. Moreover, possibilities to improve AM processability and to manipulate the resulting microstructure (c.f. grain refinement, dispersion strengthening) by adhering nanoparticles on the powders will be discussed. The effect of dry coating on the obtained powder properties along the whole AM process chain and the resulting part properties is assessed. Moreover, appropriate characterization methods for bulk solid properties of dry-coated AM powders are critically discussed.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This research presents a comprehensive methodology for calibrating Discrete Element Method (DEM) parameters governing rice grain interactions with biodegradable Polylactic Acid (PLA) components in agricultural bucket elevator systems. Rice grains, a critical global food staple requiring efficient post-harvest handling, were modeled as three-sphere clusters to accurately represent their physical dimensions (6.5 mm length), while the Hertz–Mindlin contact model provided the theoretical framework for particle interactions. The calibration process employed a multi-phase experimental design integrating Plackett–Burmann screening, steepest ascent method, and Face Central Composite Design to systematically identify and optimize critical micro-mechanical parameters for agricultural material handling. Statistical analysis revealed the coefficient of static friction between rice and PLA as the dominant factor, contributing 96.49% to system performance—significantly higher than previously recognized in conventional agricultural processing designs. Response Surface Methodology generated predictive models achieving over 90% correlation with experimental results from 3D-printed PLA shear box tests. Validation through comparative velocity profile analysis during bucket elevator discharge operations confirmed excellent agreement between simulated and experimental behavior despite a 20% discharge velocity variance that warrants further investigation into agricultural material-specific phenomena. The established parameter set enables accurate virtual prototyping of sustainable agricultural handling equipment, offering post-harvest processing engineers a powerful tool for optimizing bulk material handling systems with reduced environmental impact. This integrated approach bridges fundamental agricultural material properties with sustainable engineering design principles, providing a scalable framework applicable across multiple agricultural processing operations using biodegradable components.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Additive Manufacturing (AM) techniques, such as Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) and Stereolithography (SLA), are increasingly adopted in various high-demand sectors, including the aerospace, biomedical engineering, and automotive industries, due to their design flexibility and material adaptability. However, the tribological performance and surface integrity of parts manufactured by AM are the biggest functional deployment challenges, especially in wear susceptibility or load-carrying applications. The current review provides a comprehensive overview of the tribological challenges and surface engineering solutions inherent in FDM and SLA processes. The overview begins with a comparative overview of material systems, process mechanics, and failure modes, highlighting prevalent wear mechanisms, such as abrasion, adhesion, fatigue, and delamination. The effect of influential factors (layer thickness, raster direction, infill density, resin curing) on wear behavior and surface integrity is critically evaluated. Novel post-processing techniques, such as vapor smoothing, thermal annealing, laser polishing, and thin-film coating, are discussed for their potential to endow surface durability and reduce friction coefficients. Hybrid manufacturing potential, where subtractive operations (e.g., rolling, peening) are integrated with AM, is highlighted as a path to functionally graded, high-performance surfaces. Further, the review highlights the growing use of finite element modeling, digital twins, and machine learning algorithms for predictive control of tribological performance at AM parts. Through material-level innovations, process optimization, and surface treatment techniques integration, the article provides actionable guidelines for researchers and engineers aiming at performance improvement of FDM and SLA-manufactured parts. Future directions, such as smart tribological, sustainable materials, and AI-based process design, are highlighted to drive the transition of AM from prototyping to end-use applications in high-demand industries.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Due to the significant properties of silica, thermostatics can be enhanced using silica-additives to maximize the quality of polymer compounds and transform plastics into tailored properties. The silica additives can enhance the handling and quality performance of composites and thermoplastic polymers due to their diverse potential. Besides, using silica as an additive in different characteristics can allow granulates and powders to flow easily, minimize caking, and control rheology. On the other hand, the eruption of 3D printing technology has led to a massive new waste source of plastics, especially the polylactic acid (PLA) that is associated with the fused deposition modeling (FDM) process. In this paper, the impact on the mechanical properties when silica is mixed with waste PLA from 3D printing was studied. The PLA/silica mixtures were prepared using different blends through twin extruders and a Universal Testing Machine was used for the mechanical characterization. The result indicated that increasing silica composition resulted in the increase of the tensile strength to 121.03 MPa at 10 wt%. Similar trends were also observed for the toughness, ductility, and the yield stress values of the PLA/silica blends at 10 wt%, which corresponds to the increased mechanical property of the composite material reinforced by the silica particles. Improvement in the mechanical properties of the developed composite material promotes the effective recycling of PLA from applications such as 3D printing and the potential of reusing it in the same application.

## pqac-00000024

From text 'parrella2008comparisonbetweena pages 9-11'.

Luca Parrella, Diego Barletta, Renee Boerefijn, and Massimo Poletto. Comparison between a uniaxial compaction tester and a shear tester for the characterization of powder flowability. Kona Powder and Particle Journal, 26:178-189, Jan 2008. URL: https://doi.org/10.14356/kona.2008016, doi:10.14356/kona.2008016. This article has 40 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Parrella et al. compared uniaxial compaction tester (UCT) and ring shear tester (RST) flow functions for five powders. When UCT normal stresses were calculated only from externally applied forces, the UCT produced lower unconfined yield strengths than the RST for the more cohesive calcium carbonate powders A, B, and C; the two methods could therefore place the same powder in different flowability regions. Agreement was good for the free-flowing powder D. The authors corrected the UCT stress state by accounting for mould-wall friction and powder weight. This correction brought the UCT flow function into close agreement with the RST for calcium carbonate, but for cohesive powders A–C the agreement was satisfactory mainly at low consolidation stresses. Applying the correction requires the stress ratio K and wall-friction angle, measurable with shear cells or other testers; repose angle may estimate effective internal friction for K, while K = 0.4 may be a reasonable approximation for cohesive materials. Wall friction alone did not explain every discrepancy, particularly at high consolidation stresses. Thus, corrected UCT measurements can support industrial quality control, but an uncorrected UCT alone may not provide reliable flow functions. RST remains the more reliable and conservative method for equipment design, including silos.

## pqac-00000025

From text 'parrella2008comparisonbetweena pages 1-2'.

The article compares flow functions and unconfined yield strengths measured with a ring shear tester (RST) and a uniaxial compaction tester (UCT) for five powders. In the RST, a shear force forms a shear region in a sample consolidated by a normal force. In the UCT, powder is compacted in a cylindrical mould, the mould is removed, and the force required to break the compacted sample is measured. The methods generate different stress states and stress histories, so their strength results are not inherently directly comparable. A major source of discrepancy is wall friction in the UCT: friction at the mould wall causes the normal stress to decrease exponentially with depth, influencing the measured sample strength and flow function. After correcting or re-evaluating UCT results for wall friction, substantial agreement with RST results was obtained for calcium carbonate. For the other four food powders, agreement was observed only at low consolidation levels, while additional effects appeared at high consolidation. UCT measurements generally require higher minimum consolidation stresses to prevent failure after mould removal than shear-cell tests, which can make extrapolation toward low consolidation conditions unreliable. In particular, directly extrapolating UCT flow functions to low consolidation may underestimate powder cohesion and therefore misrepresent the unconfined yield strength comparison.

The excerpt compares conventional uniaxial compaction testing (UCT) with shear-cell methods, including the Jenike tester and Brookfield Powder Flow Tester (PFT), and discusses why their flow functions and unconfined yield strengths differ. A wall-friction correction was applied to UCT results using the effective stress equation, incorporating wall friction, the stress ratio K, powder-bed weight, and half the bed weight under the assumption that failure begins at the powder-bed midpoint. This correction brought UCT results close to PFT and Jenike results only for calcium carbonate, the easy/free-flowing powder; for iron ore, barite, and titanium dioxide it reduced, but did not eliminate, the discrepancy. The correction is therefore not universal and requires shear-cell measurements or assumptions for wall-friction and internal-friction parameters, undermining the simplicity of UCT. The excerpt reports that UCT generally produced substantially lower flow functions and unconfined yield strengths than shear testers, whereas the newly developed GUT agreed well with Jenike and PFT. Parrella et al. attributed differences between corrected UCT and Jenike results to differing stress histories during sample preparation, particularly as comparisons varied with consolidation stress. Anisotropy from retained compression history is also proposed as a cause of lower apparent shear failure in conventional UCT results.

For powders A, B, and C, agreement was good primarily at low consolidation stresses; at higher consolidation stresses, the corrected UCT functions became steeper and more linear, predicting greater unconfined yield strength than the RST. Abstract:
Recent studies evaluating the flowability and floodability of cohesive powder under conditions of consolidation, mechanical force, vibrating force, fluid force, and floodability are reviewed. The ball indentation test is an effective method for evaluating the flowability of a small amount of cohesive powder at very low stress under consolidation conditions. The environmental conditions such as temperature and humidity play an important role in the flow of cohesive powder. With regard to cohesive powder flowing under mechanical force, the FT4 powder rheometer can evaluate the powder flowability using the total energy which is related to the shear stress on the impeller blade. The vibrating capillary method and the vibrating shear tube method are effective for the measurement of the flowability of strongly cohesive powder. The test using powder discharge by air flow can assess the flowability of cohesive powder which Carr’s flowability index is an equivalent level by using mass flow rate and interstitial air pressure. Finally, the flushing of cohesive powder occurs when the interstitial air pressure and the void fraction are high. The pressure difference between the interstitial air pressure and the outside of an orifice are the dominant factors in the spouting of powder.

## pqac-00000045

From text 'arunyanart2025comprehensivedemcalibration pages 1-2'.

Pirapat Arunyanart, Nithitorn Kongkaew, and Supattarachai Sudsawat. Comprehensive dem calibration using face central composite design and response surface methodology for rice–pla interactions in enhanced bucket elevator performance. AgriEngineering, 7:240, Jul 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/agriengineering7070240, doi:10.3390/agriengineering7070240. This article has 3 citations.

The excerpt is directly relevant to DEM calibration of rice–PLA wall friction, although it does not report a specific calibrated friction angle or numerical coefficient value. The study calibrates rice interactions with biodegradable PLA components using a Hertz–Mindlin contact model, representing rice grains as three-sphere clusters with a 6.5 mm length. Its experimental calibration uses 3D-printed PLA shear-box tests and a multi-stage design involving Plackett–Burman screening, steepest ascent, and Face Central Composite Design with Response Surface Methodology. The excerpt compares a conventional cylindrical uniaxial compression tester (UCT) with the Greenwich Uniaxial Compaction Tester (GUT), focusing on cohesive powder flow and wall-friction effects. Conventional uniaxial testing suffers from wall friction and substantial measurement scatter, so the GUT was designed with a low height-to-diameter ratio to reduce friction during consolidation and improve repeatability. The GUT uses a 95 mm internal-diameter cell with a central 30 mm hole and a defined failure plane, requiring approximately 75% less sample than the UCT. Powder is consolidated under stresses from 10 to 130 kPa, including tests on iron ore containing 3% moisture. Flow-function results from GUT and UCT were compared with Brookfield Powder Flow Tester measurements at low consolidation stresses and Jenike-type shear-tester measurements at higher stresses. For the conventional UCT, the sample is compacted in a cylindrical mould, the mould is removed to create a free-standing specimen, and the maximum compressive force defines the unconfined yield strength. Because repeatability is low, at least five or six tests per stress were recommended. Wall friction was characterized using the wall friction angle or coefficient measured with the PFT, and a Janssen-style differential force balance was used to calculate the effective consolidation stress and correct for frictional effects. The excerpt explains that mould-wall friction is a major difference between conventional uniaxial compression and Jenike direct shear testing of cohesive iron ore. In uniaxial compression, wall friction reduces the effective normal stress, shifts the specimen to a different stress state, increases the voids ratio, and produces a lower yield locus and comparatively lower shear strength. Earlier correction approaches included mathematical corrections, membrane wrapping with lubrication between the membrane and mould wall, and infinite-layer preparation; although these could bring flow functions closer to Jenike results, they were material-dependent or operationally complex. The authors emphasize that eliminating wall friction alone is insufficient: the specimen must also reach the critical voids ratio through appropriate consolidation or particle rearrangement. Their proposed method uses uniform-density preparation based on undercompaction, targeting final bulk density rather than a specified normal consolidation stress. The procedure uses ten layers, with 5% undercompaction in the bottom layer and linearly varying undercompaction toward the top, to compensate for densification caused by subsequent layers. ## pqac-00000063

From text 'luddecke2026flowabilityofpowder pages 5-7'.

A. Lüddecke, H. Zetzener, and A. Kwade. Flowability of powder bed fusion metal particles with and without surface modification at very low stresses. Powder Technology, 484:122981, Dec 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2026.122981, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2026.122981. This article has 0 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt discusses wall-yield-locus intercepts, wall adhesion, and the stress dependence of the wall friction angle. A conventional wall-yield-locus construction using points above 1000 Pa intersects the shear-stress axis at 120 Pa. Interpreted as the intercept τ₀ in a relation such as τw = τ₀ + σn tan(φw), this would indicate substantial apparent wall adhesion; however, the authors state that such strong adhesion is unexpected for the investigated cohesionless particles. Low-stress wall-friction measurements instead produce a linear wall yield locus down to σw = 25 Pa, with a mean wall friction angle of 19.7°, and the authors explicitly report that the locus is not curved. The wall friction angle is stress-dependent: it decreases as wall normal stress increases, while it rises sharply as stress falls below 100 Pa. At these very low stresses, calculated φw values show considerable scatter because even a 1 Pa change in wall shear stress can cause a large angular deviation. Measurements above approximately 1500 Pa agree between standard and low-stress methods, whereas extrapolation from higher stresses can overestimate φw. The standard method’s apparent zero-stress adhesion is considered unexpected, supporting use of the low-stress method for heavy, free-flowing powders.


---

## pqac-00000064

From text 'luddecke2026flowabilityofpowder pages 4-5'.

A. Lüddecke, H. Zetzener, and A. Kwade. Flowability of powder bed fusion metal particles with and without surface modification at very low stresses. Powder Technology, 484:122981, Dec 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2026.122981, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2026.122981. This article has 0 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt directly addresses wall yield-locus behavior and apparent wall adhesion at low normal stress. Wall shear measurements are approximately linear between 2700 and 1000 Pa, allowing a wall yield locus to be constructed in that range. Below 1000 Pa, however, the locus curves disproportionately downward rather than following the higher-stress linear trend. Fitting a separate locus only to stresses below 1000 Pa produces a negative adhesion value, τad, which would imply repulsion from the wall; the authors state that this is physically implausible for the investigated cohesionless particles. They instead suggest that shear occurs in upper powder layers, so the stress acting at the wall differs from the stress calculated under the lid. Consequently, standard wall-friction measurements are unreliable for heavy stainless-steel particles at low wall normal stresses, and measurements below 400 Pa are impossible because the powder and lid weight impose a minimum stress. Extrapolating the higher-stress linear locus gives a y-axis intercept of 120 Pa, apparently indicating strong wall adhesion, although the authors emphasize that this is not expected and is likely an artifact of the low-stress measurement configuration. The excerpt does not explicitly define τw = τ0 + σn tan(φw) or quantify stress dependence of φw.


---

## pqac-00000065

From text 'pierrat1994theflowproperties pages 29-34'.

P Pierrat. The flow properties of wet granular materials. Unknown journal, 1994.

The excerpt describes the wall yield locus as the relationship between wall-normal stress and the shear stress required for a bulk solid to slide along a bunker or bin wall. It is determined experimentally by measuring the horizontal shear force needed to move the material across a plate representing the wall surface. For an ideal Coulomb material, the wall yield locus is linear and is expressed as wall shear stress equal to the coefficient of wall friction multiplied by normal stress, plus a constant wall adhesion term. In the notation used in the question, this corresponds to τw = τ0 + σn tan(φw), with τ0 representing wall adhesion and tan(φw) representing the wall-friction coefficient. The excerpt explicitly identifies Cw as the adhesion and μw as the coefficient of wall friction. It also notes that curvature in the wall yield locus is often observed, although a best-fit straight line is generally adequate for practical calculations. The passage does not specifically state that the wall friction angle increases at low normal stress, but the reported curvature indicates that wall friction may not remain constant over the full stress range. No separate low-stress dependence of φw is quantified.

## pqac-00000066

From text 'castellanos2005therelationshipbetween pages 53-55'.

A. Castellanos. The relationship between attractive interparticle forces and bulk behaviour in dry and uncharged fine powders. Advances in Physics, 54:263-376, Jun 2005. URL: https://doi.org/10.1080/17461390500402657, doi:10.1080/17461390500402657. This article has 741 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt directly supports the definition of a wall yield locus and wall adhesion within a Coulomb friction framework. For powder–wall interaction, the wall yield relation is described as a linear Coulomb-type relation involving the wall friction coefficient and a wall-adhesion term. The wall adhesion is defined as the normal force per unit area required to separate the powder from the wall. Thus, in the notation of the question, the intercept tau_w = tau_0 corresponds to the adhesion-related stress at zero normal load, while the slope is associated with the wall friction coefficient, commonly expressed through tan(phi_w). The excerpt also identifies shear-cell testing as the method used to measure Coulomb yield behavior along the wall. However, this passage does not report that the wall friction angle varies with normal stress at low stress, does not state that wall friction increases at low stress, and does not explicitly describe a curved wall yield locus. Instead, the stated wall relation is linear in normal stress. Any claim of low-stress stress dependence or curvature would therefore require additional material or experimental evidence beyond this excerpt.

## pqac-00000067

From text 'artoni2010mechanicsofdense pages 45-47'.

R Artoni. Mechanics of dense and multiphase flows of granular materials. Unknown journal, 2010.

The excerpt is relevant to wall friction and wall-yield behavior, but it does not explicitly define wall adhesion as an intercept tau_w = tau_0 + sigma_n tan(phi_w), nor does it provide a measured stress-dependent wall friction angle or a curved wall yield locus. It states that wall slip is traditionally described by a Coulomb yield criterion linking tangential and normal wall stresses through a constant friction coefficient. Importantly, it notes that the effective or apparent wall friction coefficient may vary and need not equal the microscopic wall–particle friction coefficient. The excerpt further suggests that this apparent coefficient depends on flow properties as well as local stress, which is conceptually consistent with a non-linear or curved wall-yield relationship rather than a universally linear Coulomb locus. The discussion then adopts a Navier slip condition, relating tangential velocity to its normal gradient through a slip length lambda, rather than using the Coulomb condition directly. Surface roughness is expected to reduce slip and produce a lower lambda. The text also says that high normal stress drives the behavior toward no slip. No specific claim is made here that wall friction increases at low normal stress, and no definition of wall adhesion or numerical value of tau_0 or phi_w is supplied.

From text 'hirschberg2018additivemanufacturingof pages 4-6'.

Cosima Hirschberg, Mikkel Schmidt Larsen, Johan Peter Bøtker, and Jukka Rantanen. Additive manufacturing of prototype elements with process interfaces for continuously operating manufacturing lines. Asian Journal of Pharmaceutical Sciences, 13:575-583, Nov 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajps.2018.04.007, doi:10.1016/j.ajps.2018.04.007. This article has 5 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

In the ring shear tester wall-friction experiments, lactose monohydrate exhibited less friction than mannitol against both PLA and stainless steel wall plates. The comparison between the 3D-printed PLA plate and stainless steel showed that their friction behavior diverged as normal stress increased: the difference between the two wall materials became larger at higher normal stresses. At a low normal stress of 200 Pa, however, the difference between PLA and stainless steel was small. The authors therefore concluded that, under low-stress conditions representative of small-scale setups, the choice between the printed PLA wall and stainless steel had no practical influence on powder behavior. The PLA wall plate was produced by 3D printing without post-treatment; the article notes that solvent-vapor or mechanical post-treatment could smooth the surface and reduce wall friction. These findings were relevant because the experimental setups used 3D-printed polymeric walls rather than the stainless steel commonly used in industrial equipment.

{"answer": "## Literature Review: Tilting-Plate Wall Friction and Uniaxial Compression Testing at Low Consolidation Stresses

### Part (a): Inclined-Plane / Tilting-Plate Wall Friction

#### 1. Principle and Comparison with Standard Shear Cells

In an inclined-plane or tilting-plate wall friction test, a powder-filled ring or sled rests on a wall coupon and the inclination is increased quasi-statically until gross sliding initiates. The static wall friction coefficient is obtained as μ_s = tan θ_s for negligible adhesion (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000065). This contrasts with standard shear-cell wall friction methods—Jenike translational (ASTM D6128) and Schulze ring shear (ASTM D6773)—which drag pre-consolidated powder across a wall coupon under controlled normal loads and measure the resulting shear stress to construct a wall yield locus (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006).

The two approaches do not automatically produce identical results. The inclined-plane measures incipient static sliding at a single low normal stress set by gravity, while shear cells produce a locus over a range of controlled normal stresses. Pillai et al. (2007) showed that an on-line wall friction tester, conceptually related to a sled geometry, produced significantly higher wall friction angles than a Jenike tester, in part because longer shear displacements allowed particle embedding into the wall surface—an effect the limited 10 mm Jenike stroke could not replicate (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000007).

#### 2. Low Normal Stress Behavior (50–500 Pa)

At low normal stress, standard shear cells encounter fundamental limitations. Jenike shear-flow measurements below approximately 1 kPa consolidation stress are generally considered impractical (pqac-00000004). Han (2011) compared Jenike and Schulze ring shear wall friction tests for PE pellets on stainless steel and aluminum wall plates and found that the two testers agreed well at higher pressures (4600 and 10 000 Pa) when wall roughness was comparable, but at 500 Pa the Schulze RST gave substantially larger wall friction angles than the Jenike tester, with the authors unable to determine which method was more accurate (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006). This divergence at low stress is practically important because low wall pressures occur near silo outlets.

A tilting-plate test is naturally well-suited to the 50–500 Pa regime because gravity supplies both normal and tangential forces without requiring subtraction of two small load-cell signals. By varying specimen mass and ring area, normal stresses can be tuned directly to the desired range.

#### 3. Stress Dependence of Wall Friction Angle and Wall Adhesion

The wall yield locus is generally expressed as τ_w = τ_0 + σ_n tan(φ_w), where τ_0 is the wall adhesion (the shear stress intercept at zero normal stress) and φ_w is the wall friction angle (pqac-00000065, pqac-00000066). For an ideal Coulomb material the locus is linear, but curvature is commonly observed in practice (pqac-00000065). The wall friction angle is stress-dependent: it increases as wall normal stress decreases, rising sharply below approximately 100 Pa. At very low stresses, even a 1 Pa change in wall shear stress can produce a large angular deviation, so scatter in reported φ_w values becomes considerable (pqac-00000063). Lüddecke et al. (2026) showed that for cohesionless stainless steel powder, extrapolating a wall yield locus fitted above 1000 Pa produced an apparent wall adhesion intercept of 120 Pa, which was physically implausible. Direct low-stress measurements down to 25 Pa instead showed a linear wall yield locus with a mean wall friction angle of 19.7° and no true adhesion, demonstrating that apparent wall adhesion can be an artifact of high-stress extrapolation (pqac-00000063, pqac-00000064).

#### 4. Wall Friction on Polymers (PLA, PETG, ABS, Nylon), Stainless Steel, and Glass

Direct measurements of powder wall friction on 3D-printed polymer surfaces are sparse but beginning to appear. Hirschberg et al. (2018) fabricated a PLA wall plate for a Schulze ring shear tester and measured wall friction of lactose monohydrate and mannitol. At a low normal stress of 200 Pa, the difference between untreated 3D-printed PLA and stainless steel was small and considered to have no practical influence. At higher normal stresses, however, the PLA–stainless steel difference increased, with the rough printed PLA surface producing higher friction (pqac-00000068, pqac-00000049). The authors noted that solvent-vapor or mechanical post-treatment of PLA could reduce wall friction.

For granular materials on PLA, Arunyanart et al. (2025) measured the coefficient of static friction between rice grains and 3D-printed PLA at 0.324–0.574 (corresponding nominally to 18–30°), identifying this as the dominant DEM calibration parameter with 96.49% contribution to angle-of-repose prediction (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046). These values are specific to rice grains and cannot be transferred directly to fine powders without independent measurement.

The following table summarizes wall friction measurement methods and their low-stress capabilities:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

#### 5. Start Angle of Thin Powder Layers on Inclined Planes (Pouliquen h_stop/h_start Curves)

For non-cohesive granular media on rough inclined planes, Pouliquen and Forterre (2001) established that both the starting angle θ_start(h) and stopping angle θ_stop(h) depend on layer thickness h, with the two curves separated by approximately one degree of hysteresis. Both critical angles increase strongly as the layer becomes thin—for very thin layers the angles diverge—and approach finite, thickness-independent limits for large h. For glass beads, the empirical fit parameters were δ_1 = 21°, δ_2 = 30.7°, δ_3 = 22.2°, and L = 0.65 mm (pqac-00000019). The stopping thickness h_stop(θ) is the inverse function of θ_stop(h) and defines the deposit remaining after flow ceases at a given inclination. A non-local friction-based model reproduces this behavior, predicting θ_stop = tan⁻¹[μ_Y(H + z_0)/H] with hysteresis arising from distinct yield and stability thresholds (pqac-00000018).

For **cohesive powders**, the framework is significantly modified. Gans, Pouliquen, and Nicolas (2020) showed that cohesion introduces an additional thickness-dependent yield stress, expressed as h sin θ_start = μh cos θ_start + h_c, where h_c = τ_c/(φρ_g g) is a cohesion length representing the maximum thickness of a vertically self-supporting layer. Thinner layers require a larger angle to initiate flow, and the influence of cohesion diminishes for thick layers (pqac-00000016). De Ryck and Louisnard (2013) extended this to finite-width channels, finding that cohesion raises the steady-flow onset angle above the angle of repose, creates a surface plug zone, and strongly interacts with channel-width confinement—even weak cohesion can measurably increase the avalanche angle as channel width decreases (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022). Mandal, Nicolas, and Pouliquen (2021) showed that the effective cohesion during flow is not controlled solely by interparticle adhesion but also depends on particle stiffness and inelasticity; cohesion broadens the hysteresis between starting and stopping conditions and promotes shear-band instability (pqac-00000021).

---

### Part (c): Uniaxial / Unconfined Compression Tests at Low Consolidation Stress

#### 1. Published Apparatus Designs

The following table compares the principal published uniaxial and low-stress testing apparatus:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**Williams and Birks split-mould tester.** The original Williams unconfined compression method uses a segmented split mould (H/D = 3.5) with successive compaction increments. The unconfined yield strength is plotted against 1/N (where N is the number of layers) and extrapolated to 1/N = 0, representing infinitely many zero-thickness increments to minimize wall-friction bias. More than ten layers are generally used. The titanium dioxide flow function agreed closely with Jenike shear-cell results (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012).

**Parrella uniaxial compaction tester (UCT).** Parrella et al. (2008) compared a cylindrical UCT with a Schulze ring shear tester for five powders. Without wall-friction correction, the UCT systematically gave lower unconfined yield strengths and could place powders in different flowability classes than the RST. Applying a Janssen-type correction with lateral stress ratio K = 0.4 and independently measured wall friction angle brought the UCT flow function into close agreement with the RST for calcium carbonate, but only at low consolidation stresses for the more cohesive food powders. At high consolidation stresses, additional mechanisms beyond wall friction (particle fragmentation, orientation changes) caused divergence (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030).

**Freeman Advanced Uniaxial Powder Tester (AUPT).** This instrument uses a 41 mm diameter × 100 mm tall specimen (H/D ≈ 2.44), consolidates at 0.5 mm/s, and crushes at 0.2 mm/s. The analysis assumes uniform stress transmission and does not explicitly correct for wall friction (pqac-00000010).

**Greenwich Uniaxial Tester (GUT).** Developed by Salehi et al. (2019), the GUT uses a 95 mm internal-diameter cell with a low H/D ratio, a central 30 mm punch-out hole, and a defined failure plane. It requires approximately 75% less sample than a conventional UCT and reportedly achieves substantially better agreement with Jenike and Brookfield PFT results, though it operates at consolidation stresses of 10–130 kPa (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000058).

**Johanson Indicizer.** This device uses a cylindrical cell with a two-part upper piston. The sample is consolidated for a preset time, the lower support is removed, and the inner piston is pushed down to failure. The measured empirical strength is multiplied by approximately 2.2 to estimate unconfined yield strength. While faster than Jenike testing, multiple researchers questioned whether the corrected stress represents true unconfined yield strength, and comparisons found that the Indicizer often produced appreciably lower unconfined yield strengths and arching diameters than Jenike and Peschl shear cells (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000034).

**Brookfield Powder Flow Tester (PFT).** Though technically an annular shear cell rather than a uniaxial tester, the Brookfield PFT provides a low-stress benchmark. Its standard-volume cell operates over approximately 0.3–4.8 kPa, with the lowest setting at 0.3 kPa (300 Pa), which partially overlaps the user's 0.2–2 kPa target range (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035).

#### 2. Height-to-Diameter Ratio

The H/D ratio is a critical design parameter. Wall friction produces a Janssen-type exponential decay of vertical stress with depth, so a large H/D creates nonuniform consolidation and variable bulk density along the specimen (pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060). Minimizing H/D reduces this gradient but, below a critical value, the failure plane intersects the end plates and invalidates the measurement. While a 45° failure-plane assumption suggests H/D ≥ 1, experimental evidence indicates that end-plate slippage effects become negligible only when H/D exceeds approximately 2 (pqac-00000011). Published values range from H/D = 2.0 (Chen et al. 2017, using 80 mm diameter × 160 mm height) to H/D = 3.5 (Williams) to H/D ≈ 2.44 (Freeman AUPT) (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000010). For the user's proposed 20 mm diameter × 40 mm column, H/D = 2.0, which is at the minimum recommended value.

#### 3. Mould Wall Friction During Consolidation

Wall friction during uniaxial consolidation is the primary source of discrepancy between uniaxial and shear-cell methods. The applied vertical stress decreases exponentially with depth according to a Janssen force balance, shifting the specimen to a lower effective consolidation stress, increasing the voids ratio, and producing a lower yield locus than achieved in shear cells (pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060). This results in uniaxial testing generally indicating apparently higher flowability (lower unconfined yield strength) than shear testing (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000030).

Correction approaches include: (i) the Janssen-based Parrella correction using K = 0.4 and independently measured wall friction angle (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000030); (ii) the Williams infinite-layer extrapolation, which mathematically removes the layer-based wall-friction contribution (pqac-00000012); (iii) Chen et al.'s (2017) undercompaction technique, targeting final bulk density rather than specified normal stress, using ten layers with 5% undercompaction at the bottom and linear variation to the top (pqac-00000059); and (iv) the POSTEC tester's flexible membrane, which reduces specimen–die friction by wrapping the sample (pqac-00000008).

For the user's 20 mm × 40 mm split-mould design, wall friction will be particularly important because the small diameter increases the wall-contact-area-to-cross-section ratio. Using a PLA split mould where the wall is removed before failure testing is advantageous; measuring wall friction on the same PLA surface with the tilting-plate test can provide the correction inputs.

#### 4. Uniaxial Strength vs. Shear-Cell Unconfined Yield Strength and ffc

### Part (a): Inclined-Plane / Tilting-Plate Wall Friction

#### 1. Principle and Comparison with Standard Shear Cells

In an inclined-plane or tilting-plate wall friction test, a powder-filled ring or sled rests on a wall coupon and the inclination is increased quasi-statically until gross sliding initiates. The static wall friction coefficient is obtained as μ_s = tan θ_s for negligible adhesion (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000065). This contrasts with standard shear-cell wall friction methods—Jenike translational (ASTM D6128) and Schulze ring shear (ASTM D6773)—which drag pre-consolidated powder across a wall coupon under controlled normal loads and measure the resulting shear stress to construct a wall yield locus (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006).

The two approaches do not automatically produce identical results. The inclined-plane measures incipient static sliding at a single low normal stress set by gravity, while shear cells produce a locus over a range of controlled normal stresses. Pillai et al. (2007) showed that an on-line wall friction tester, conceptually related to a sled geometry, produced significantly higher wall friction angles than a Jenike tester, in part because longer shear displacements allowed particle embedding into the wall surface—an effect the limited 10 mm Jenike stroke could not replicate (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000007).

#### 2. Low Normal Stress Behavior (50–500 Pa)

At low normal stress, standard shear cells encounter fundamental limitations. Jenike shear-flow measurements below approximately 1 kPa consolidation stress are generally considered impractical (pqac-00000004). Han (2011) compared Jenike and Schulze ring shear wall friction tests for PE pellets on stainless steel and aluminum wall plates and found that the two testers agreed well at higher pressures (4600 and 10 000 Pa) when wall roughness was comparable, but at 500 Pa the Schulze RST gave substantially larger wall friction angles than the Jenike tester, with the authors unable to determine which method was more accurate (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006). This divergence at low stress is practically important because low wall pressures occur near silo outlets.

A tilting-plate test is naturally well-suited to the 50–500 Pa regime because gravity supplies both normal and tangential forces without requiring subtraction of two small load-cell signals. By varying specimen mass and ring area, normal stresses can be tuned directly to the desired range.

The wall yield locus is generally expressed as τ_w = τ_0 + σ_n tan(φ_w), where τ_0 is the wall adhesion (the shear stress intercept at zero normal stress) and φ_w is the wall friction angle (pqac-00000065, pqac-00000066). For an ideal Coulomb material the locus is linear, but curvature is commonly observed in practice (pqac-00000065). The wall friction angle is stress-dependent: it increases as wall normal stress decreases, rising sharply below approximately 100 Pa. At very low stresses, even a 1 Pa change in wall shear stress can produce a large angular deviation, so scatter in reported φ_w values becomes considerable (pqac-00000063). Lüddecke et al. The authors noted that solvent-vapor or mechanical post-treatment of PLA could reduce wall friction.

These values are specific to rice grains and cannot be transferred directly to fine powders without independent measurement.

The following table summarizes wall friction measurement methods and their low-stress capabilities:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

For non-cohesive granular media on rough inclined planes, Pouliquen and Forterre (2001) established that both the starting angle θ_start(h) and stopping angle θ_stop(h) depend on layer thickness h, with the two curves separated by approximately one degree of hysteresis. Both critical angles increase strongly as the layer becomes thin—for very thin layers the angles diverge—and approach finite, thickness-independent limits for large h. For glass beads, the empirical fit parameters were δ_1 = 21°, δ_2 = 30.7°, δ_3 = 22.2°, and L = 0.65 mm (pqac-00000019). Thinner layers require a larger angle to initiate flow, and the influence of cohesion diminishes for thick layers (pqac-00000016). state.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A 25 mm OD tube with a 21 mm bore and a helical flight ends in a 3 mm outlet; a NEMA 11 stepper turns it at 1-109 rpm, servos tilt it 0-90 degrees, a solenoid taps it, and doses fall onto a 0.1 mg analytical balance. We record a dosing fingerprint (mass per revolution vs tilt and speed, mass per tap, afterflow, no-flow fraction) on 13 powders (NaCl, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg, silicon, rice flours, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 dihydrate, fumed silica and others) and calibrate a LIGGGHTS DEM twin. Property labels from handbooks limit our models (angle-of-repose ranges 6-16 degrees wide), so we are designing ten small in-house tests built around the doser, each using a few grams and run on the same jar and day as the fingerprint: (1) heap angle of repose on a 20 mm fixed pedestal on the balance, photographed in silhouette; (2) bulk and tapped density in a 10 mL Class A cylinder filled by the auger and tapped by a cam drop of 3 mm at 250 taps/min, column height read by camera; (3) a servo tilting plate with an IMU: wall friction of a 25 mm powder-filled ring at 70-450 Pa on PLA, stainless steel and glass, and the start angle of 1-5 mm powder layers; (4) particle size and shape from backlit images with a Raspberry Pi HQ camera and a 0.12-1.8x zoom lens; (5) a 25 mm cup with 1-6 mm orifice discs and a servo gate emptying onto the balance (Beverloo fit, smallest orifice that flows, with and without taps); (6) humidity chambers held by saturated salt solutions (MgCl2, Mg(NO3)2, NaCl, KCl, silica gel) with SHT45 sensors, weighing uptake and dosing before and after; (7) a 40 mm by 15 mm rotating drum driven by the doser's stepper, 1-20 rpm; (8) unconfined yield strength of a 20 mm by 40 mm column from a split mould after 0.2-2 kPa consolidation, crushed by a lead-screw platen on a 100 g load cell; (9) a blade spreading a 0.1-0.2 mm layer over a 100 x 30 mm coupon at 10-100 mm/s; (10) a Faraday cup (aluminium cup in a grounded can) with a femtoamp op-amp charge amplifier under the doser outlet. For tests (3) and (8): what does the literature report on (a) inclined-plane or tilting-plate measurements of powder wall friction (a powder-filled ring or sled on a tilting wall coupon) compared with Jenike (ASTM D6128) and Schulze ring-shear (D6773) wall-friction tests, especially at low normal stress (50-500 Pa) where shear cells struggle, the stress dependence of the wall friction angle, wall adhesion, and typical wall friction angles of powders on polymers (PLA, PETG, ABS, nylon), stainless steel and glass; (b) the start angle of thin powder layers on inclined rough planes versus layer thickness (Pouliquen h_stop/h_start curves) for cohesive powders; (c) uniaxial or unconfined compression tests of powder columns at low consolidation stress (0.2-5 kPa): published apparatus (Williams and Birks, Parrella, Freeman, the Brookfield PFT, the Ezi-Tester, Johanson Indicizer), the height-to-diameter ratio, mould wall friction during consolidation, how uniaxial strength compares with shear-cell unconfined yield strength and flow function ffc, and the smallest consolidation stresses at which strength has been measured reliably.

## Literature Review: Tilting-Plate Wall Friction and Uniaxial Compression Testing at Low Consolidation Stresses

### Part (a): Inclined-Plane / Tilting-Plate Wall Friction

#### 1. Principle and Comparison with Standard Shear Cells

In an inclined-plane or tilting-plate wall friction test, a powder-filled ring or sled rests on a wall coupon and the inclination is increased quasi-statically until gross sliding initiates. The static wall friction coefficient is obtained as μ_s = tan θ_s for negligible adhesion (ramirezgomez2025testapparatusfor pages 8-10, pierrat1994theflowproperties pages 29-34). This contrasts with standard shear-cell wall friction methods—Jenike translational (ASTM D6128) and Schulze ring shear (ASTM D6773)—which drag pre-consolidated powder across a wall coupon under controlled normal loads and measure the resulting shear stress to construct a wall yield locus (khala2021characterisingpowderflow pages 38-42, han2011comparisonofwall pages 1-3).

The two approaches do not automatically produce identical results. The inclined-plane measures incipient static sliding at a single low normal stress set by gravity, while shear cells produce a locus over a range of controlled normal stresses. Pillai et al. (2007) showed that an on-line wall friction tester, conceptually related to a sled geometry, produced significantly higher wall friction angles than a Jenike tester, in part because longer shear displacements allowed particle embedding into the wall surface—an effect the limited 10 mm Jenike stroke could not replicate (pillai2007comparisonbetweenthe pages 4-5, pillai2007comparisonbetweenthe pages 1-2).

#### 2. Low Normal Stress Behavior (50–500 Pa)

At low normal stress, standard shear cells encounter fundamental limitations. Jenike shear-flow measurements below approximately 1 kPa consolidation stress are generally considered impractical (khala2021characterisingpowderflow pages 38-42). Han (2011) compared Jenike and Schulze ring shear wall friction tests for PE pellets on stainless steel and aluminum wall plates and found that the two testers agreed well at higher pressures (4600 and 10 000 Pa) when wall roughness was comparable, but at 500 Pa the Schulze RST gave substantially larger wall friction angles than the Jenike tester, with the authors unable to determine which method was more accurate (han2011comparisonofwall pages 3-7, han2011comparisonofwall pages 7-7, han2011comparisonofwall pages 1-3). This divergence at low stress is practically important because low wall pressures occur near silo outlets.

A tilting-plate test is naturally well-suited to the 50–500 Pa regime because gravity supplies both normal and tangential forces without requiring subtraction of two small load-cell signals. By varying specimen mass and ring area, normal stresses can be tuned directly to the desired range.

#### 3. Stress Dependence of Wall Friction Angle and Wall Adhesion

The wall yield locus is generally expressed as τ_w = τ_0 + σ_n tan(φ_w), where τ_0 is the wall adhesion (the shear stress intercept at zero normal stress) and φ_w is the wall friction angle (pierrat1994theflowproperties pages 29-34, castellanos2005therelationshipbetween pages 53-55). For an ideal Coulomb material the locus is linear, but curvature is commonly observed in practice (pierrat1994theflowproperties pages 29-34). The wall friction angle is stress-dependent: it increases as wall normal stress decreases, rising sharply below approximately 100 Pa. At very low stresses, even a 1 Pa change in wall shear stress can produce a large angular deviation, so scatter in reported φ_w values becomes considerable (luddecke2026flowabilityofpowder pages 5-7). Lüddecke et al. (2026) showed that for cohesionless stainless steel powder, extrapolating a wall yield locus fitted above 1000 Pa produced an apparent wall adhesion intercept of 120 Pa, which was physically implausible. Direct low-stress measurements down to 25 Pa instead showed a linear wall yield locus with a mean wall friction angle of 19.7° and no true adhesion, demonstrating that apparent wall adhesion can be an artifact of high-stress extrapolation (luddecke2026flowabilityofpowder pages 5-7, luddecke2026flowabilityofpowder pages 4-5).

#### 4. Wall Friction on Polymers (PLA, PETG, ABS, Nylon), Stainless Steel, and Glass

Direct measurements of powder wall friction on 3D-printed polymer surfaces are sparse but beginning to appear. Hirschberg et al. (2018) fabricated a PLA wall plate for a Schulze ring shear tester and measured wall friction of lactose monohydrate and mannitol. At a low normal stress of 200 Pa, the difference between untreated 3D-printed PLA and stainless steel was small and considered to have no practical influence. At higher normal stresses, however, the PLA–stainless steel difference increased, with the rough printed PLA surface producing higher friction (hirschberg2018additivemanufacturingof pages 4-6). The authors noted that solvent-vapor or mechanical post-treatment of PLA could reduce wall friction.

For granular materials on PLA, Arunyanart et al. (2025) measured the coefficient of static friction between rice grains and 3D-printed PLA at 0.324–0.574 (corresponding nominally to 18–30°), identifying this as the dominant DEM calibration parameter with 96.49% contribution to angle-of-repose prediction (arunyanart2025comprehensivedemcalibration pages 8-11, arunyanart2025comprehensivedemcalibration pages 1-2, arunyanart2025comprehensivedemcalibration pages 11-12). These values are specific to rice grains and cannot be transferred directly to fine powders without independent measurement.

The following table summarizes wall friction measurement methods and their low-stress capabilities:

| Method | Principle | Typical normal stress range | Low-stress capability | Key limitations | Reference examples |
|---|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Jenike translational shear cell (ASTM D6128) | Powder is consolidated against a representative wall coupon and translated over a limited stroke; steady wall shear stress versus wall-normal stress defines the wall yield locus, commonly represented as $\tau_w=\tau_0+\sigma_n\tan\phi_w$. | Generally moderate stresses; conventional measurements below about **1 kPa** are difficult or impractical. | Poor for **50–500 Pa** because lid/sample weight, force resolution, preparation, and limited displacement become dominant. | Operator-sensitive; short shear travel (about 10 mm) may not establish long-displacement conditioning or particle embedding; extrapolating a high-stress locus can create spurious adhesion or low-stress friction values. | (khala2021characterisingpowderflow pages 38-42, pillai2007comparisonbetweenthe pages 4-5, luddecke2026flowabilityofpowder pages 5-7, pierrat1994theflowproperties pages 29-34) |
| Schulze annular ring shear cell (ASTM D6773) | An annular powder bed undergoes effectively unlimited relative displacement over a wall coupon; controlled normal loads produce the wall yield locus and steady wall-friction angle. | Commonly about **0.5 kPa upward**, depending on cell, powder density, lid, and transducer; specialized procedures can extend below 1 kPa. | Better than Jenike at low stress, but agreement deteriorated at **500 Pa**: Schulze RST gave substantially higher wall-friction angles than Jenike for PE pellets. | Minimum load from lid and powder; possible nonuniform stress or shear above rather than at the coupon; very small shear forces amplify angular uncertainty. Tester-specific results require validation below 1 kPa. | (han2011comparisonofwall pages 3-7, han2011comparisonofwall pages 7-7, khala2021characterisingpowderflow pages 42-46, luddecke2026flowabilityofpowder pages 4-5) |

| Inclined-plane or tilting-plate sled/ring | A powder-filled ring or locked-particle sled rests on a wall coupon; inclination is increased until gross sliding starts. For negligible adhesion, $\mu_s=\tan\theta_s$; with adhesion, $mg\sin\theta_s=\mu_w mg\cos\theta_s+\tau_0A$. | Set by specimen areal load; readily designed for approximately **50–500 Pa** by changing ring mass, ballast, and contact area. | Well suited to low normal stress because gravity supplies both normal and tangential forces without subtracting two small load-cell signals. Multiple loads permit fitting $\mu_w$ and $\tau_0$. | Measures static incipient sliding, not necessarily steady wall friction; failure may occur inside the powder rather than at the wall; unknown real contact/load distribution, tilt acceleration, stick–slip, edge drag, and cohesion can bias $\tan\theta$. It is not automatically equivalent to ASTM wall testing. | (ramirezgomez2025testapparatusfor pages 8-10, pierrat1994theflowproperties pages 29-34, castellanos2005therelationshipbetween pages 53-55) |
| Proposed doser-based tilting coupon with 25 mm powder-filled ring | Fill and level the same ring reproducibly, apply calibrated ballast, tilt PLA, stainless-steel, or glass coupons quasi-statically, and detect first sustained displacement by camera/IMU. Fit all loads directly to $F_t=\tau_0A+\mu_wF_n$ rather than reporting only $\tan\theta$. | Intended **70–450 Pa**; a 25 mm ring has area $4.91\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2}$, so this corresponds to total normal forces of about **0.034–0.221 N** or mass equivalents of **3.5–22.5 g** at zero tilt. | Strong match to the doser’s operating regime and small sample budget; same-day replication can reveal humidity, conditioning, print orientation, and surface-fouling effects. Include at least four loads and both start and steady-sliding angles. | Must distinguish interfacial slip from internal shear using underside imaging or a powder-marked coupon; actual $\sigma_n=(mg\cos\theta)/A$ changes during tilt; ring-wall drag must be eliminated. Treat results as an application-specific low-stress wall-slip index until cross-calibrated against an RST at overlapping **300–500 Pa**. | PLA-versus-stainless differences were small at **200 Pa** for lactose and mannitol, while untreated printed PLA roughness mattered increasingly at higher stress; rice–PLA static-friction coefficients of **0.324–0.574** correspond nominally to **18–30°**, but are not transferable powder-independent constants (arunyanart2025comprehensivedemcalibration pages 8-11, hirschberg2018additivemanufacturingof pages 4-6) |


*Table: Comparison of standardized shear cells and gravity-driven tilt methods for measuring powder–wall friction, emphasizing the 50–500 Pa regime and how the proposed 25 mm ring should be interpreted and validated.*

#### 5. Start Angle of Thin Powder Layers on Inclined Planes (Pouliquen h_stop/h_start Curves)

For non-cohesive granular media on rough inclined planes, Pouliquen and Forterre (2001) established that both the starting angle θ_start(h) and stopping angle θ_stop(h) depend on layer thickness h, with the two curves separated by approximately one degree of hysteresis. Both critical angles increase strongly as the layer becomes thin—for very thin layers the angles diverge—and approach finite, thickness-independent limits for large h. For glass beads, the empirical fit parameters were δ_1 = 21°, δ_2 = 30.7°, δ_3 = 22.2°, and L = 0.65 mm (pouliquen2001frictionlawfor pages 5-8). The stopping thickness h_stop(θ) is the inverse function of θ_stop(h) and defines the deposit remaining after flow ceases at a given inclination. A non-local friction-based model reproduces this behavior, predicting θ_stop = tan⁻¹[μ_Y(H + z_0)/H] with hysteresis arising from distinct yield and stability thresholds (artoni2010mechanicsofdense pages 65-67).

For **cohesive powders**, the framework is significantly modified. Gans, Pouliquen, and Nicolas (2020) showed that cohesion introduces an additional thickness-dependent yield stress, expressed as h sin θ_start = μh cos θ_start + h_c, where h_c = τ_c/(φρ_g g) is a cohesion length representing the maximum thickness of a vertically self-supporting layer. Thinner layers require a larger angle to initiate flow, and the influence of cohesion diminishes for thick layers (gans2020cohesioncontrolledgranularmaterial pages 8-9). De Ryck and Louisnard (2013) extended this to finite-width channels, finding that cohesion raises the steady-flow onset angle above the angle of repose, creates a surface plug zone, and strongly interacts with channel-width confinement—even weak cohesion can measurably increase the avalanche angle as channel width decreases (ryck2013depthandminimal pages 33-35, ryck2013depthandminimal pages 12-14, ryck2013depthandminimal pages 1-3). Mandal, Nicolas, and Pouliquen (2021) showed that the effective cohesion during flow is not controlled solely by interparticle adhesion but also depends on particle stiffness and inelasticity; cohesion broadens the hysteresis between starting and stopping conditions and promotes shear-band instability (mandal2021flowsofcohesive pages 4-5).

### Part (c): Uniaxial / Unconfined Compression Tests at Low Consolidation Stress

#### 1. Published Apparatus Designs

The following table compares the principal published uniaxial and low-stress testing apparatus:
